briefs.cervicitis:
Cervicitis and Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

chlamydia and gonorrhea at the cervix, then ascent to the upper tract · treat on the exam finding, before the test returns; the threshold is low by designIs there cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, is she pregnant, and does she meet an admission criterion?

DiagnosisPracticeManagement
Bottom line

Both are clinical diagnoses, usually treated at the visit. Send nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for both organisms at the same time, but do not wait for it in pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), or in cervicitis when she is at increased risk. The aim is to interrupt transmission and prevent the sequelae: PID, ectopic pregnancy, infertility and chronic pelvic pain.

  • Cervicitis: two major signs, a mucopurulent discharge and a friable cervix that bleeds easily on swab contact. Most prevalent under 25; frequently asymptomatic, or an abnormal discharge and intermenstrual bleeding.
  • Presumptive cervicitis treatment: for women at increased risk, if follow-up cannot be ensured, or if NAAT is not possible; deferring until results is an option at lower risk. Doxycycline covers C trachomatis; ceftriaxone, considered when she is at risk for gonorrhea or lives in a community where gonorrhea prevalence is high, covers N gonorrhoeae.
  • Increased risk includes: under 25, a new partner, or a partner with concurrent partners or a sexually transmitted infection (STI).
  • PID: a presumptive clinical diagnosis with a deliberately low threshold.
  • Minimum criteria for PID: a sexually active young woman or other woman at risk, pelvic or lower abdominal pain, no other identified cause, and any one of cervical motion tenderness (CMT), uterine tenderness or adnexal tenderness.
  • Additional criteria: oral temperature above 38.3 °C, mucopurulent cervical discharge or friability, abundant white blood cells on saline microscopy, a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein, documented gonococcal or chlamydial infection. They support the diagnosis and raise its specificity.
  • Absent CMT does not reassure in cervicitis: CMT marks ascent, and early or low-burden infection lacks it.
  • Pregnancy: azithromycin replaces doxycycline; PID in pregnancy means admission.

The threshold is low because treatment prevents the sequelae and delay causes them. Managing the alternatives (ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, ovarian cyst, torsion) is not impaired by starting antimicrobials: treating early carries no diagnostic penalty, treating late a permanent one.

Diagnosis
Pelvic pain or discharge in a young woman: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tell
Cervicitis (chlamydia, gonorrhea)Age under 25, high-risk sexual behavior; asymptomatic most commonly; the two organisms often coinfectMucopurulent discharge, friable cervix; no CMT needed
PIDAscending gonococcal, chlamydial or vaginal-flora infectionCMT with mucopurulent discharge
Ectopic pregnancy, can't missAmenorrhea then unilateral painPositive human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) with an empty uterus; a pregnancy test is always mandatory
Tubo-ovarian abscessA complication of PID rather than a separate diseasePalpable or sonographic adnexal mass; admit
Ovarian torsionSudden severe unilateral pain with an ovarian massNausea and vomiting, usually afebrile, absent or reduced Doppler flow, though preserved flow does not exclude it when suspicion is high
AppendicitisPeriumbilical pain that migratesMcBurney point tenderness, no cervical findings
PyelonephritisAscending urinary infectionCostovertebral angle tenderness with pyuria
Chlamydial urethritisDysuria that reads as cystitisLeukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative, with cervical discharge
Screening The USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) recommends screening every sexually active woman under 25 for chlamydia and gonorrhea, and older women at increased risk, annually by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidance, with NAAT for both organisms, even with no discharge and a normal exam. Most infections are silent, and treating them prevents PID and its sequelae.
Practice
  1. 17-year-old girl has had sudden pelvic pain since yesterday Sexually active; no other cause found cervical motion tenderness purulent cervical discharge no adnexal mass on bimanual exam T 39 °C · HR 104/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Start empiric antibiotics now → pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness and no other cause meets the minimum criteria, so presumptive treatment starts now. The purulent discharge and an oral temperature above 38.3 °C add specificity, and above 38.5 °C she meets an admission criterion. A pelvic ultrasound is normal in uncomplicated disease and delays treatment; the amplification test is positive in only about half, so neither result could change today's decision
  2. 22-year-old woman has 1 week of vaginal discharge New male partner 2 months ago mucopurulent discharge at the cervical os cervix bleeds on contact with the swab no cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness Afebrile · urine pregnancy test negative → Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline → mucopurulent discharge and a cervix that bleeds easily on swab contact are the two major signs. Under 25 with a new partner she is at increased risk, so presumptive treatment for both organisms is given at the visit while the nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) is pending: doxycycline for chlamydia, and ceftriaxone for gonorrhea, considered when she is at risk or lives in a high-prevalence community. Sexually active and under 25, she is in the group screened annually for gonorrhea (CDC). Azithromycin plus doxycycline covers chlamydia twice and leaves gonorrhea untreated
  3. 23-year-old woman has 3 days of lower abdominal pain Mucopurulent vaginal discharge for 2 weeks No pregnancy or delivery in the past year uterine and adnexal tenderness cervical motion tenderness T 38.4 °C · HR 96/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Pelvic inflammatory disease → pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness and no other cause meets the minimum criteria: the infection has ascended from the cervix. Cervicitis alone lacks that tenderness, and postpartum endometritis needs a recent delivery
  4. 24-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has a positive screening test for chlamydia First pregnancy; no symptoms Same test negative for gonorrhea normal pelvic exam Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg → Azithromycin → azithromycin 1 g orally once is the recommended regimen in pregnancy; doxycycline is not the recommended regimen in pregnancy and is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because of tooth discoloration, and ceftriaxone alone treats gonorrhea, not chlamydia. A test of cure about 4 weeks after treatment is recommended in pregnancy
  5. 19-year-old woman has 4 days of pelvic pain and fever Sexually active; urine pregnancy test negative cervical motion and left adnexal tenderness 6-cm tubo-ovarian abscess on transvaginal ultrasound T 38.9 °C · HR 108/min · BP 118/72 mm Hg → Admit for intravenous antibiotics → a tubo-ovarian abscess is a hospitalization criterion, and more than 24 hours of inpatient observation is recommended: intravenous antibiotics first, with drainage if the abscess fails medical therapy. Outpatient oral therapy is for women without an admission criterion, and laparotomy is not the first step ⚠︎
  6. 21-year-old woman has 4 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner no costovertebral angle tenderness mucopurulent cervical discharge on speculum exam Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive · nitrite negative → Chlamydial urethritis with cervicitis → leukocyte esterase without nitrite in a sexually active woman should prompt a pelvic exam for chlamydia: atypicals do not reduce nitrate, and the cervical discharge reframes the urinary tract infection. Send a NAAT; a urine culture often shows no growth. Cystitis lacks the discharge, and pyelonephritis brings costovertebral angle tenderness
  7. 24-year-old woman has 2 days of lower abdominal pain Copper intrauterine device placed 2 years ago cervical motion and uterine tenderness no adnexal mass on ultrasound T 37.9 °C · HR 90/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Treat and leave the device in place → the intrauterine device does not need to be removed: treat with close clinical follow-up, and consider removal only if there is no improvement within 48 to 72 hours. All contraceptive methods can be continued during treatment
  8. 25-year-old woman has fever and lower abdominal pain 3 days after vaginal delivery Membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery uterine tenderness foul-smelling lochia T 38.7 °C · HR 104/min · BP 116/70 mm Hg → Clindamycin plus gentamicin → fever with uterine tenderness days after delivery, after prolonged rupture of membranes, is polymicrobial ascent from the lower genital or gastrointestinal tract; first-line treatment is intravenous clindamycin plus gentamicin, not an STI regimen. Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline treats gonorrhea and chlamydia, and TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is not a regimen for gonorrhea, chlamydia or PID
  9. 22-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has 2 days of pelvic pain Intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound mucopurulent cervical discharge cervical motion and adnexal tenderness T 38.1 °C · HR 98/min → Hospitalize for intravenous antibiotics → pregnancy is itself a hospitalization criterion: suspected ascending infection in pregnancy carries a high risk of maternal morbidity and preterm delivery, so she is admitted for intravenous antimicrobials in consultation with an infectious disease specialist. Outpatient therapy is wrong whatever the regimen because pregnancy mandates admission, and azithromycin alone also leaves gonorrhea untreated
  10. 17-year-old girl has 2 days of right upper quadrant pain that worsens with deep breaths Treated last week for lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness gallbladder normal on ultrasound T 38.2 °C · HR 96/min · chest radiograph normal → Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome → the pelvic infection reached the liver capsule: perihepatitis with violin-string adhesions, which gives right upper quadrant pleuritic pain. Cholecystitis would show on the gallbladder ultrasound, and a lower lobe pneumonia on the chest radiograph ⚠︎
  11. 18-year-old woman has worsening pelvic pain 72 hours after starting outpatient therapy Ceftriaxone injection, then oral doxycycline and metronidazole persistent cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness T 38.6 °C · HR 106/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Admit for intravenous therapy and reassess the diagnosis → no clinical improvement within 72 hours of outpatient intramuscular or oral therapy calls for hospitalization, assessment of the antimicrobial regimen and additional diagnostics, including consideration of diagnostic laparoscopy for an alternative diagnosis. Extending the oral course or adding azithromycin keeps a failing outpatient plan
  12. 19-year-old woman has a positive screening test for chlamydia No symptoms; routine screening at her annual visit Same test negative for gonorrhea normal pelvic exam Afebrile · urine pregnancy test negative → Doxycycline alone → confirmed chlamydia alone in a nonpregnant patient is treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days; ceftriaxone is not needed once gonorrhea has been tested for and excluded. Treat partners from the previous 60 days, and retest her about 3 months after treatment; a test of cure is not advised
  13. 20-year-old woman has 4 days of lower abdominal pain Starting outpatient treatment today; no other cause found Last sexual intercourse 3 weeks ago, with her only partner cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness T 37.9 °C · urine pregnancy test negative → Evaluate, test and treat the partner now → pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness and no other cause is presumptive PID, so anyone who had sexual contact with her during the 60 days before symptom onset is evaluated, tested and presumptively treated for chlamydia and gonorrhea, regardless of the cause or pathogens found; if her last intercourse was more than 60 days ago, the most recent partner is treated
  14. 16-year-old girl has sudden severe right pelvic pain that began 3 hours ago Vomited twice tender right adnexal mass no cervical motion tenderness or cervical discharge Afebrile · HR 112/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Ovarian torsion → sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting, an adnexal mass and no fever: Doppler ultrasound may show absent or reduced flow, though complete loss of flow is not necessary and preserved flow does not exclude it when suspicion is high; then laparoscopy. Ascending pelvic infection brings cervical motion tenderness and discharge, and a ruptured cyst gives sudden pain without a persisting mass ⚠︎
  15. 17-year-old girl is starting treatment today for pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness Cervical NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia sent No earlier testing for sexually transmitted infections T 38.0 °C · urine pregnancy test negative → HIV and syphilis → every woman with this diagnosis is tested for gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV and syphilis, and a woman with chlamydial or gonococcal infection is retested 3 months after treatment. Hepatitis C testing alone misses the infections recommended here ⚠︎
How NBME framed it: question 1

16-year-old girl seen with her mother for a routine health maintenance visit Previously healthy; takes no medications; immunizations current Periods come every 28 to 35 days, irregularly; last one 3 weeks ago No tobacco, alcohol or illicit drugs One male partner for the past year; no condom use Family history: breast cancer in her mother at age 40 height 163 cm · weight 65 kg · body mass index 25 kg/m² · vital signs normal breasts: no masses, no nipple discharge external genitalia normal; no vaginal discharge sexual maturity rating 5 for breasts and pubic hair

Most appropriate screening test now?

Competing answers
  • Mammography: her mother's breast cancer at 40 is the planted cue; but routine mammography starts at 40, not in adolescence.
  • Fasting serum glucose: a body mass index of 25; but that alone does not meet the adolescent diabetes screening bar, which needs overweight plus risk factors such as insulin resistance.
  • Hemoglobin concentration: irregular menses are the planted cue; but routine iron deficiency anemia screening is not a US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation.

Down to two: a Pap smear or chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT. NAAT for both organisms: every sexually active woman under 25 is screened, even with no discharge and a normal exam, because most infections are silent and the two often coinfect. Cervical cytology starts at 21 whatever the sexual history. Each decoy carried a planted cue, and the key named the test in full.

Management
Regimens and follow-up (CDC 2021)
SituationRegimenThen
Cervicitis, presumptiveDoxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days; consider adding ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once if she is at risk for gonorrhea or in a high-prevalence community (1 g at 150 kg or more)Treat partners for the infection identified or suspected. If an organism is identified: partners from the previous 60 days, and retest her at 3 months
Chlamydia alone, confirmedDoxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 daysNo test of cure if not pregnant; retest about 3 months after treatment
Chlamydia in pregnancyAzithromycin 1 g orally once; amoxicillin 500 mg 3 times daily for 7 days is the alternativeTest of cure about 4 weeks after treatment
GonorrheaCeftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once (1 g at 150 kg or more); doxycycline as above if chlamydia is not excludedTest of cure only for pharyngeal infection, at 7 to 14 days; retest at 3 months
PID, outpatientCeftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once, plus doxycycline 100 mg and metronidazole 500 mg, each orally twice daily for 14 daysNo improvement within 72 hours: hospitalize, reassess the regimen and the diagnosis, consider diagnostic laparoscopy
PID, inpatientCeftriaxone 1 g intravenously (IV) every 24 hours with doxycycline 100 mg and metronidazole 500 mg, each orally or IV every 12 hours; or cefotetan 2 g IV every 12 hours, or cefoxitin 2 g IV every 6 hours, with doxycycline; doxycycline orally when possible, because IV infusion is painfulOral doxycycline and metronidazole usually within 24 to 48 hours of improvement, completing 14 days; an abscess failing medical therapy is drained
When to admit By provider judgment and any of: a surgical emergency such as appendicitis cannot be excluded, tubo-ovarian abscess (more than 24 hours of inpatient observation), pregnancy, severe illness, nausea and vomiting or an oral temperature above 38.5 °C, inability to follow or tolerate an oral regimen, or no response to oral therapy. Adolescence is not itself a criterion; the same thresholds apply as for adults. All contraceptive methods can be continued, and an intrauterine device does not need removal; consider removing it if there is no improvement within 48 to 72 hours.
Partners and retesting Treat partners. For PID, everyone with sexual contact in the 60 days before symptom onset is evaluated, tested and presumptively treated for chlamydia and gonorrhea, whatever her results; if her last intercourse was more than 60 days ago, the most recent partner is treated. Partners abstain until both are treated. Retest a woman with chlamydial or gonococcal infection 3 months after treatment, whether or not partners were treated.
Pearls The low threshold is the guideline, not a shortcut: clinical diagnosis carries a positive predictive value of only 65 to 90% for salpingitis, and that is accepted deliberately. Only about half of acute PID has a positive gonorrhea or chlamydia test, so a negative test never excludes it. Metronidazole joined the routine outpatient regimen in 2021 for anaerobic coverage; older item banks may key ceftriaxone plus doxycycline alone. Quinolones are no longer recommended because of gonococcal resistance. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis is PID that reached the liver capsule, with right upper quadrant pleuritic pain. Sterile pyuria in a sexually active woman (leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative) should prompt a pelvic exam for chlamydia.
Common wrong answers Azithromycin plus doxycycline: looks like dual therapy, but both cover the same organism; it doubles atypical coverage and leaves N gonorrhoeae untreated, the classic wrong pairing. TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole): not a regimen for gonorrhea, chlamydia or PID; gonococcus is multidrug-resistant, and United States strains are not adequately susceptible to penicillin, tetracycline and older macrolides, with fluoroquinolones dropped in 2007 for resistance. A negative nitrite: it cannot rule out infection that nitrite was never sensitive for, because atypicals do not reduce nitrate. Pelvic ultrasound first: normal in uncomplicated PID; it delays the only intervention that prevents sequelae. Urine culture: right class of test, wrong compartment. Contraception: appropriate care, but prevention rather than treatment of an established infection. A Pap smear for a sexually active 16-year-old: cervical cytology starts at 21 whatever the sexual history.
Pairs with Part II Cervical Screening: the Age-21 Floor: is she 21 or older, or is she due only for chlamydia and gonorrhea screening? Part I Ectopic Pregnancy must always be considered with PID: both present as acute pelvic pain in a reproductive-age woman, and one test settles the fork. Ask: what is the pregnancy test?
Transferable rule

When a diagnosis is clinical or presumptive and the sequelae are irreversible, treat at the visit and send the tests at the same time; the confirmatory test is documentation rather than management. Ask what the pending test could change today, and treat if the answer is nothing.
